samples.question: This image shows five square framed panels standing side by side; count them 1 to 5 from left to right. Every panel contains exactly three straight opaque bands of the same thickness, each band in its own solid colour, and every band runs the whole way across its own panel. Inside each panel the three bands meet in three separate crossings, one for each pair of bands. At a crossing one band passes in front of the other: the band in front keeps its colour running unbroken through the crossing, and the band behind is interrupted there and reappears on the far side. Solid bands lying flat on a table can only be stacked in one top-to-bottom order, so in a physically possible panel the three crossings agree with a single stacking order: one band is in front at both of its crossings, one band is behind at both of its crossings, and the third is in between. In exactly one panel the three crossings instead run in a cycle, so that the first band is in front of the second, the second is in front of the third, and the third is in front of the first; that panel is woven and no single stacking order can explain it. The four other panels are each consistent with a stacking order. Nothing else marks the answer: the colours of the bands, which colour happens to be in front at any single crossing, the directions of the bands, where in the panel the crossings fall, the number of bands, the amount of ink and the size of every part are the same kind in every panel and carry no information. Only whether the three crossings of a panel can all hold at once decides the answer. Which numbered panel is the woven one whose three crossings cannot be produced by any single stacking order of its three bands? Answer with exactly one of: panel-1, panel-2, panel-3, panel-4, panel-5.
